clue.text: Novelist reviewing The Role of the Superego

blocks.note: Will Self is an English novelist
reviewing books or plays is the work of criticism

explanation.surface: A novelist writing a critique of a psychology book called The Role of the Superego.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letters dress the definition up as a book title under review.
explanation.definitionFit: In Freud's model the superego is the inner judge, so its function is to pass judgment on one's own conduct.

clue.text: Baking has a sickly spread

indicators.note: something sickly is out of sorts, so the letters before it are put into disorder

blocks.note: the two words rearranged
dye or ink that spreads is said to have run, past tense ran

explanation.surface: A baked dish comes with an unappetising topping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baking' looks like cooking, but it means scorching hot. 'Sickly spread' looks like a sugary topping.
explanation.definitionFit: Like the great North African desert, which is famously scorching hot weather.

clue.text: Unlovely cravat, in part-synthetic fibre

indicators.note: in part means the letters are found within a portion of the preceding words

blocks.note: the run straddles the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: An ugly necktie made partly of man-made material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part-synthetic' reads as one adjective for the cravat; split it so 'in part' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a trademarked elastic man-made material, used in stretchy clothing such as sportswear.

clue.text: Time learner's invested in task? It's a laugh

indicators.note: to be invested in something is to be put inside it

blocks.note: a chore is a routine task
T is the abbreviation for time
L is for learner, as on a British L-plate

explanation.surface: A student puts hours into a piece of homework, and finds the whole thing a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of learner's means is. A British learner driver displays an L-plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A gleeful, snorting chuckle is one particular kind of laugh.

clue.text: I'll give you that note (credit card's declined)

indicators.note: a declined card is knocked back, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, with the S

explanation.surface: A shopper conceding a point after a message arrives saying their card was refused at the till.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are concessions that the other person is right and one's own view was mistaken.

clue.text: Crowd invasion when area lost by Liverpool striker

indicators.note: something lost by a person no longer belongs to them, so that letter drops out of the name

blocks.note: Ian Rush was Liverpool's prolific Welsh centre-forward of the 1980s
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A pitch invasion at Anfield after the Liverpool forward loses the ball in the penalty area.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the A from Ian Rush's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden flooding in of people, water or air is a surge into a place.

clue.text: That's me off making a contribution

blocks.note: a contraction of I am
parting means leaving, going off

explanation.surface: A departing guest's farewell after chipping in to the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the whole phrase as I'M PARTING, a cheery goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to give or share something, such as knowledge, so it means giving a share.

clue.text: Monkey around, affectedly impersonating Danny Dyer?

indicators.note: something done affectedly is put on and unnatural, so the letters take on an artificial order

blocks.note: taken as written
C is short for circa, Latin for around

explanation.surface: Someone clowning about with a put-on accent while doing an impression of an actor.
explanation.walkthrough: Danny Dyer is a London actor famous for his strong cockney accent; the question mark flags him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a fake working-class London accent put on by someone imitating cockney speech.

clue.text: Pulse half missing, getting terribly cool

indicators.note: with half gone, only the front portion of the pulse word survives

blocks.note: a chickpea is a pulse, an edible seed of a legume

explanation.surface: A heartbeat that drops half its beats would leave a patient terribly cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' suggests a heartbeat, but here it is the food sense: a dried legume seed. Drop the back four letters of CHICKPEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stylish and fashionable is described as cool, and the word for elegant style fits that sense.

clue.text: Europe cast unfairly as 'place lacking atmosphere'

indicators.note: something treated unfairly is mishandled, so the letters are knocked out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sneering critic unfairly portrays Europe as a dull place with no atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking atmosphere' sounds like a put-down of a dull venue, but it is literal: no air.
explanation.definitionFit: The void beyond Earth's air envelope literally has no gaseous layer around it.

clue.text: French city declared bust

indicators.note: declared means spoken out, so the city name is heard rather than read

blocks.note: Brest is a port city in Brittany

explanation.surface: A French city has been officially declared bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like the bankrupt sense to go with 'declared', but it is the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is the chest of a person, especially a woman's bosom.

clue.text: What one familiar with Wagner does in audition, offering ornamentation

indicators.note: an audition is a hearing, so the phrase is taken by its sound

blocks.clueFragment: What one familiar with Wagner does
blocks.note: someone who knows Wagner knows his four-opera Ring cycle

explanation.surface: An opera singer auditioning shows off their familiarity with Wagner and adds a flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Audition' suggests a singer trying out, but it simply means a hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: A piercing jewel worn through the nostril is a piece of facial decoration.

clue.text: Dumbly disrespect, ignoring old in favour of oneself

indicators.note: ignoring one letter means it is passed over and dropped from the word
in favour of names the letter preferred, which takes the dropped one's place

blocks.note: insolence is rude disrespect
O is a standard abbreviation for old
I is the word for oneself when speaking

explanation.surface: A selfish person mutely snubs their elders, putting themselves first.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the O of INSOLENCE to I.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something dumbly means without speaking, which is acting without a sound.

clue.text: Doomed to receive porcelain that's leaking

blocks.note: if you are in for something, trouble is coming your way
Ming is fine Chinese porcelain from the Ming dynasty

explanation.surface: A cracked vase is bound to be dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaking' looks like a crack in the porcelain; it means passing on secrets.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who leaks secrets passes confidential information to others, telling on people.

clue.text: Slight: 'Trust in you? Not entirely'

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the quoted words is used, a run sitting inside them

blocks.note: the run straddles the three words

explanation.surface: A wounded lover answers 'Do you trust me?' with a slightly hurtful 'Not entirely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something slight is small in size or amount, very little indeed.

clue.text: Enthusiast with excellent muscle tone

blocks.note: first meaning: a fan or devotee, as in a film fan
second meaning: informal for physically fit and toned

explanation.surface: A keen gym-goer who is in great shape.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for a devoted fan of a subject and slang adjective for a muscular, toned body.

clue.text: Labour: 'Foot could be PM'

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters might be rearranged into something else

blocks.note: taken as written
F is the abbreviation for foot, the unit of length

explanation.surface: A Labour party slogan claiming Michael Foot could become prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Foot led Labour in the 1980s, making 'Foot' look like a name. Arthur Balfour was a Conservative prime minister of 1902 to 1905.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Balfour held office as Britain's prime minister early in the twentieth century.

clue.text: Spooner's curious admirer delivers a kitchen utensil

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words trade places

blocks.note: prying means nosy or curious, and a fan is an admirer

explanation.surface: A nosy fan turns up bearing a cooking pot as a present.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallow long-handled pan for cooking food in hot fat is a standard piece of kitchen equipment.

clue.text: Shunning company around urinals

indicators.note: around suggests the letters are moved about into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy man keeping his distance from others in the gents.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inward-looking and isolated from others, like an island, means avoiding outside contact.

clue.text: Tentatively ask Iris to show affection

indicators.note: a tentative approach is unsure and uncertain, so the letters wander from their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy suitor nervously asks Iris whether he may give her a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretend kiss near the cheek without contact is a light social greeting displaying warmth.

clue.text: Open, concealing nothing, unusually blunt

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it inside, so one piece goes within another
unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters of the word after it are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An unusually frank person who is open and hides nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' and 'concealing nothing' look like describing a candid person; 'Open' is a verb, as of a door.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw back the bar fastening a door is to open it, releasing the lock.

clue.text: Nightingale in the city?

blocks.note: first meaning: the first name of the nursing pioneer Nightingale
second meaning: the Italian city on the Arno, capital of Tuscany

explanation.surface: A songbird singing somewhere in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nightingale' suggests the bird, but it is the Crimean War nurse, who was named after the Italian city where she was born.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous nurse was given the name of her birthplace, the Tuscan capital.

clue.text: Writer's voice has sounds of hesitation

blocks.note: to voice an opinion is to say it, and having your say is having a voice
er is the noise a speaker makes while hesitating

explanation.surface: An author's speech is full of ums and ers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorothy L Sayers was an English writer of detective novels featuring Lord Peter Wimsey.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy L Sayers was a celebrated crime novelist, so her surname names an author.

clue.text: At end of twelvemonth, Norse pine

blocks.note: twelve months make a year
N is the abbreviation for Norse

explanation.surface: A Viking homesick for a whole year, or a Scandinavian pine tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like the conifer suggested by 'Norse', but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine is to long or ache for something absent, a wistful desire.

clue.text: Drunken harlot embraceth corrupted Zion, even

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters of the first word lurch out of order
to embrace is to wrap one's arms round, so one set of letters goes around the other
something corrupted is spoilt from its proper form, so the letters of the second word are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mock-biblical line about a drunken whore leading Zion into sin.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic 'embraceth' sets an Old Testament tone, but it just means goes around. 'Even' looks like an adverb; it is the adjective meaning flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A level, flat surface lies parallel to the ground, like a line drawn across the horizon.

clue.text: I doubt that easy life is without limits

indicators.note: limits are the edges of each word, so losing them keeps only the inner letters

blocks.note: the inner pair of letters
the inner pair of letters

explanation.surface: A sceptic doubts that a life of ease can ever be boundless.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a scornful retort expressing disbelief, like saying 'fat chance' or 'yeah, right'.

clue.text: Conservative journalist, grown up with Sun, made restitution

indicators.note: up here means stirred or disturbed, so the word before it is jumbled

blocks.note: the political right is the conservative side
ED is short for editor, the senior journalist
the word grown rearranged
S is the abbreviation for Sun, as in Sunday

explanation.surface: A Tory columnist on the Sun newspaper grew up and made amends.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid, which makes 'journalist ... Sun' look like a newspaper reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Correcting injustices one has done means making amends, compensating for the harm caused.
